**1. The property, in Lean** [read: the file at `b66d9cd53c4b`; `r` is a `CheckedRun`, `ω` the wire map, `keep` what the wired program returns].

```lean
/-- the roots the wired program opens gate `g` under -/
def CheckedRun.rootsWired (g : ℕ) : List Msg :=
  if g ∈ cutBlock ω r.rb ∧ (r.s.prog.wired ω keep).Boundary (cutBlock ω r.rb) g = false then
    iroots r.x r.seen r.ρ
  else r.s.roots

def CheckedRun.AddressHoldsWired (S : Address) (i g : ℕ) : Prop :=
  r.Counted h ∧ r.RowAt h S i ∧ (r.ReadsRegisteredWired h ω keep S g ∨ r.ReadsInteriorWired h ω keep S g)

def AddressesWired : Prop :=
  ∃ addr : ℕ → Address,
    (∀ i, (addr i).place = (addr (ω i)).place ∧ (addr i).slot = (addr (ω i)).slot) ∧
      ∀ r : CheckedRun, r.Ok h → ∀ i, r.s.prog.Needs r.b i → r.AddressHoldsWired h ω keep (addr i) i (ω i)
```

How it differs from `Addresses` (`SlotsAt.lean:322`), in five points.

- **The runs are the same.** `r.Ok h` is the accepted run of the verifier as it is, over the members' programs side by side; the wired program enters only through `ω` and `keep` [read: `CheckedRun.Ok`]. So the premise is about what the verifier accepts today and not about a second verifier.
- **An address is a side-by-side gate's.** It is asked at each gate `i` the unit's proof block needs side by side, the gate its session holds, and it is the address of `ω i` at the wired program. A unit needs gate `g` at the wired program only where it needs side by side a gate `i` with `ω i = g` [read: `Prog.needs_wired`, `Rewire.lean`].
- **One record a gate.** The roots are `rootsWired (ω i)`: the replay block's interior record where `ω i` is in the replay block with its moved gates removed and is not at that block's boundary in the wired program (it is no output the wired program returns, no input, and no gate outside the block reads it), else the statement's [read: `Reveal.rootsAt`, `Prog.refIn`, which the generic statement fixes].
- **The two arms name an entry by what it is under the roots**, `entryAt roots S.slot = keyAt roots K`, where `Addresses` had `S.slot.key = K` and `S.slot.sized = false`. A writer's own port and a reader's registered read of it name one entry of the interior record under two keys, so one slot serves both: `entryAt_interior_port` [run: compiled, `r20261111-182715-0114`].
- **One place and one slot for gates sent to one gate**, the first conjunct. The frame's code fixes the place and where it checks by position alone (`Code.place`, `Code.at_`, `Code.ownAt`), so the conjunct is forced by the interface [read: `Code.lean`]. The port is each gate's own.

**2. Your guess, corrected** [read, except where tagged].

- "Each gate has one address per record that commits it, and the two records agree where both commit it": no agreement between records enters. At the wired program each gate a unit needs is opened under exactly one record, the one `rootsWired` names. A wired read is opened by its reader too, at its writer's gate and under the interior record: the reader's session holds the row, so the reader has an opening of it, in its own port. "Only its writer's block opens it" is true of the gates a block holds and false of the openings.
- The rest of the guess stands: an output the wired program returns is opened under the statement's roots, and a registered value at the root round 2 reads it under.
- The model's `stmtOk` never runs the design check [read: `SpotFlock.stmtOk`], so every condition on the wires is a condition on `h` and none comes from the accepted run. That is why the three shapes of section 5 matter.

**3. Two reads of one committed leaf by one unit: as first compiled, no; as committed now, yes.**

- At `a999e9bf82` the property gave one address a wired gate with one port a unit [run: `r20261111-182715-0114`, exit 0]. > 1. **What ran.** Stock vLLM (`0.28.1rc1.dev472+gd9105ea80`, none of our code in the engine) serving GLM-5.3 with FP8 weights as one engine across 8 H200s. Its flags: `--tensor-parallel-size 8 --max-model-len 131072 --max-num-seqs 256 --seed 0`. Everything else was vLLM's default. [read: the run's `meta.json` and `server.log:11`]
> 2. **Workload.** The first 651 requests of our 128k mix: 482 ShareGPT chats, 122 multi-turn chats, 29 long prompts (9.7k to 32k tokens) and 18 near 128k. Prompts: median 58 tokens, mean 3,433, longest 130,808; the 47 long ones hold 95% of the prompt tokens. Output caps: median 256, mean 286, at most 875. 332 requests sample at temperature 0.7 with a seed and 319 are greedy. [ran: counts over the run's `plan.jsonl`]
> 3. **Load and the number.** Requests were sent at their planned times, at a nominal 1.6 a second (4 times the mix's planned rate), whether or not the engine kept up; no concurrency was held. On average 85 ran at once (at most 211) while 237 waited (at most 450). 279.5 = 2,172,672 computed tokens / (971.8 s × 8 GPUs). 91.8% of those are prompt tokens: output alone is 22.9 tokens a GPU-second. One pass of 16 minutes. [read: the pass's `meta.json`; ran: `metrics.jsonl`]
> 4. **No latency bound was held.** The run overloads the engine on purpose, to find its ceiling. Of the 600 requests that finished, the time to first token was 330 s at the median and 576 s at the 99th percentile; 51 of the 651 were cancelled unfinished after a 600 s wait; 1 of 651 met the harness's own bound (first token within 2 s, then 80 ms a token). Prefix caching was on (10.8% of prompt tokens came from it; the cache was emptied before the pass), chunked prefill on (8,192 tokens a step), speculative decoding off. [read: `table.json`, `server.log:21`, `:14`]
> 5. **Speculative decoding was excluded on purpose, as scope, and never measured.** Daniel's list of 7 Nov (PRF-461, item 8) said: include it, or say why not and what it would change. Our worker answered on Sat 7 Nov 4:07 PM PST: exclude it and say so in the post; proofs took that into the post's goal. I found no decision of Daniel's on that answer. GLM-5.3 ships its own draft layer, which vLLM can serve. Serving it verified needs a circuit for that layer, decode rows of 1+k positions, a new sampler circuit above temperature 0, the accepted count as a derived value or as advice (about log2(k+1) bits a decode row), and a scheduler model, which today refuses it. The worker's estimate, with nothing run: 1.05 to 1.45 times the output tokens a second per request at saturation, and 0.95 to 1.15 times the requests. [read: PRF-461's comments; the code lines in section 2]

### The brief, revised (same text as the note)

### Which serving rate the 300 GB goal is read at, and how to measure it

Draft, Wed 11 Nov 2026.

#### Recommendation

Read the 300 GB goal at the highest rate at which a tuned, unmodified vLLM server holds a stated latency bound, as MLPerf's Server test measures it, on our production-like workload and one public workload, and quote its rate with no latency bound beside it as the ceiling. Measure the same server with speculative decoding on, as vLLM's recipe for this model has it, and let the measured gain decide whether it comes into the audited circuit, which cannot express it today.

#### 1. Our two numbers

**Assumed: utilization 0.4.** One field of the cost model, set on 26 Oct with no measurement behind it. For GLM-5.3 on an H200 it implies 4,994 tokens a GPU-second (my arithmetic from the cost model's partly modeled inputs).

**Measured: 279.5 tokens a GPU-second.**

- Server: unmodified vLLM at its defaults on our eight-H200 machine, one copy of GLM-5.3 (FP8 weights) across all eight cards, context limit 131,072 tokens. Prefix caching on (repeated prompt beginnings are not recomputed), speculative decoding off.
- Workload: 651 requests modeled on production traffic. Prompts: median 58 tokens, longest 130,808; the 47 longest hold 95% of the prompt tokens. Outputs: mean 286.
- Load: random arrivals at four times the rate the server keeps up with, so requests queue. Doubling the rate again computed no more.
- Counted: every prompt and output token computed. 92% are prompt tokens. Output alone is 22.9 tokens a GPU-second.
- **No latency bound was held.** The median request waited 330 seconds for its first token. One request in 651 met MLPerf's bound for DeepSeek-R1: first token within 2 seconds, 80 ms per output token.

**The gap.** The measured run is utilization 2.2% (my arithmetic), 18 times below 0.4. SemiAnalysis's public benchmark has GLM-5, the same-sized predecessor, on eight H200s at 572 to 852 tokens a GPU-second (8,000-token prompts, 1,000-token outputs, the SGLang engine): utilization 4% to 7% (my arithmetic). So 0.4 is six to nine times above the best public rate, and our server two to three times below it. Both factors are rough: engine, model revision and workload differ.

#### 2. What a performance engineer would want to see

**Metrics**

- Throughput at a stated bound on time to first token and time per output token, never alone. MLPerf Server reports the highest random-arrival rate at which the 99th percentile of each stays inside the bound. SemiAnalysis reports tokens a second per GPU at a stated output speed per user.
- The curve from light load to saturation, with the no-bound rate (MLPerf Offline) as its ceiling.
- Prompt and output tokens stated apart. SemiAnalysis's rate counts both together, as ours does.

**Workload**

- Public and named. It moves the rate as much as tuning: prompt tokens are computed thousands at a time, output tokens one per request per step. MLPerf: long documents (mean 9,400 tokens in, 680 out). SemiAnalysis: random tokens, 1,000 in and 1,000 out, or 8,000 and 1,000. vLLM's benchmark command: recorded chats (ShareGPT, BurstGPT) or random tokens.

**Serving configuration**

- Engine and version, precision, how the model is split across cards, context limit, batch limits, tokens processed per step, cache size, prefix caching, speculative decoding, repetitions.
- Evidence of tuning: the engine's published recipe, or a sweep.

#### 3. Speculative decoding

A small part of the model guesses the next few tokens; the full model checks them in one pass and keeps the matches.

- **vLLM.** The version we pin and the current release (0.33) support it, and GLM-5.3 ships the guessing layer. vLLM's recipe for GLM-5 on eight H200s turns it on with three guessed tokens, "for low latency & small batch size". Our run otherwise matches that recipe closely.
- **Measurements.** SemiAnalysis, GLM-5 on H200, 1,000 tokens in and out: 329 tokens a GPU-second with it against 145 without, at the same 41 tokens a second per user. Gains shrink as load grows. The vLLM lane expects little change in our 279.5, which is mostly prompt tokens (its estimate, nothing run).
- **Who serves with it.** Google says AI Overviews does. SemiAnalysis writes that "most frontier labs" have enabled it for DeepSeek's model. MLPerf allows it in its Interactive test only.
- **Our earlier decision.** On 7 Nov you asked the vLLM lane to "either include it or state why it's excluded and what it would change." It answered the same day: "exclude it from the SPOT scope and say so in the post. Nothing on our side can express it today." Neither the lane nor I found a ruling of yours since.
- **What it touches** (the vLLM lane's account, not checked by me). A new registered circuit: the guessing layer, steps that check several tokens at once, and a new sampling circuit. The count of accepted guesses becomes a computed value or charged advice. The replay code refuses such a step today (I read that). How proof blocks would be drawn: not read.

#### 4. Options

Exfiltration figures are GB a year over the world's compute at an audit budget of 10%, for the best designed configuration (not built). They follow the rate in proportion. Each range runs from the verifier with two changes not yet landed to the verifier as it is.

| Rate the goal is read at | What it measures | For and against, from a performance engineer | Exfiltration figure | What it takes to run | Main risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Assumed utilization 0.4** (4,994 tokens a GPU-second) | Nothing. | For: none. Against: no source, and at least six times the best public rate for this model family on these cards. | 3,406 to 5,445 GB (the cost model's, modeled) | Nothing. | We report missing the goal 11 to 18 times over, at a rate no server reaches. |
| **B. Saturation, no latency bound, vLLM's defaults** (279.5, measured) | The most tokens this server computed, whatever the wait. | For: a real run, and MLPerf Offline is the same idea. Against: one request in 651 inside the bound, no tuning, one repetition, two to three times below the public rate. | 191 to 305 GB (my arithmetic) | Done. | It meets the goal only because the server is slow. |
| **C. Latency bound as MLPerf Server defines it, vLLM's defaults** | The highest random-arrival rate at which the 99th percentile of both latencies stays inside the bound. | For: the field's standard, and what production holds. Against: still not tuned. A 130,000-token prompt cannot start in 2 seconds, so the bound must grow with the prompt (MLPerf gives its long documents 6 seconds). | Below 124 to 198 GB (my arithmetic, from our run at 182 tokens a GPU-second, where a third of requests met the bound). On short chats alone, with 16 in flight at once, 99% met it at 64 tokens a GPU-second: 44 to 70 GB (my arithmetic). | A search over arrival rates with no audit attached: a few hours of the eight-H200 machine (my estimate). | The lowest rate of all, so it flatters us most. |
| **D. Tuned server at a latency bound, on our workload and one public workload, with speculative decoding measured beside it** (recommended) | The rate an engineer would recognise and can set beside public tables. | For: answers "is it tuned?", follows vLLM's recipe, and it is still an upper reading: it assumes the server stays that busy all year. Against: more runs. It is not the server our audit checks today, which the vLLM lane calls "further from tuned than this run" (its prefix caching is off). With speculative decoding on, our audit cannot check it at all yet. | 390 to 930 GB if we reach the public 572 to 852 (my arithmetic; another engine and workload). With speculative decoding: no figure, because the circuit changes. | The same search on two workloads, twice: six to eight hours of the machine (my estimate). It ends Sat 14 Nov 12:07 AM PST, no other eight-card machine is planned, and the audit's own runs need it too. | vLLM at our version may not start with speculative decoding (untested). And if we reach the public rates, we report missing the goal by 1.3 to 3 times. |

**What would change the recommendation**

- If the goal must hold for batch jobs too: read it at the tuned server's rate with no latency bound, which is higher.
- If the machine has no free hours before it ends: quote the range 190 to 930 GB.
- If speculative decoding adds under a tenth on our workload: leave it out and say so. If much more: read the goal with it on, which needs the new circuit first.

#### 5. What I could not establish

- Who chose 0.4, and from what.
- What limits our server. Its cards read as busy 99.9% of the run yet compute 2.2% of their ceiling, and nobody has profiled it.
- Any rate at which our workload meets a latency bound, any run with speculative decoding, a second repetition.
- What a top lab's own servers reach. None publish it.
- Whether the figure stays proportional to the rate on another workload. Every "my arithmetic" cell assumes it.
- A configuration the vLLM lane would defend as tuned. It lists what a tuned server would change and has tried none of it.

Why 64 and not 32:
- 64 is the combine's column block (`COMBINE_COLS`), so on a split row each column end reads one values unit's output row whole and the combine is the template served today; at 32 the combine becomes a new template at half the width and twice the count, and at 128 the column end needs a second form [read: `sparse_mla_split.py:494-503`, `chain_rows.py:26-28`: "a wire reads its writer's row whole, which is why a split ends in column blocks"].
- 64 costs 416 GB less than 128 in the model and 3% to 13% more GPU-seconds than the head block; 32 would save about 200 GB more [guess, from the two tables' difference] for twice the units and committed rows a block, and its saving is not on the table of record.
- Under 32 a short first block's values unit has no row over 111 bytes and Flock's composer refuses it; at 32 and 64 every values unit and column end is accepted [run: `/tmp/headsplit/design.py`, `interface.check_proof_block` at GLM-5.3's statics; read: `verity/commitments/windows/interface.py:320-345`].
The partition chooses the width, so 128 and 32 stay one line of a partition away.

**Why the figure falls by more than half, from the cost model's code** [read: lane notes `tools/wf_width.py:73-84` `cutg`, `tools/plan/plansearch.py:81-99` `kappa_rule`]. The model samples each type of proof block in proportion to the bits one block commits (k_t = κ n_t (b_t + ℓ_t) / B), and the head's key block is both the widest type (16,544 bits) and the most expensive to prove (a 2^27 Flock block), so it takes the sampled proofs' budget. After the split the 2^27 unit commits 1,216 bits, so it is sampled about 13 times less often, and the 16,384 bits of O sit on units of a quarter (128 columns) or an eighth (64) of the block's proving seconds, so the same budget proves a larger share of the replay blocks. So the boundary registration must commit the keys' value columns a second time, in column blocks; nothing ties the two copies today (#8917's caveat, CIR-235).
- **Refused, and refused the same for today's whole key blocks** [run: the same script on today's chain]:

### The brief, whole (note `20261111T1922Z-draft-network-prototype-brief`)

#### Network certification: what to show a lab

For Daniel, on his question of Wed 11 Nov, 9:42 AM PST. From the proofs lane. The network accounting lane's lead has not read this draft; the lane's own answer of today is quoted in part 8. Bracketed marks are explained under Sources.

##### The answer

**The state.** A lab's security engineer asks how many bytes a compromised inference server can get out in a year, against the size of the weights. For GLM-5.3 today the honest answer is every byte of every response. GLM-5.3 has been served behind the network certifier, but nothing yet proves that a served response is the model's output, and everything else rests on that. [relayed 20]

**The prototype.** Build one red-team demonstration on GLM-5.3: a modified inference server tries each named way to send a planted random string out through the network certifier. For each way it reports the bits recovered outside beside the bits the audit's bound charged, and three arms at one full load (no certifier, an honest server, the attacking server) give the cost. Run it on our eight-H200 node, and use VCF's cluster (the one you call the B300 cluster) for the timing test and for a certifier on a second machine. [judgment]

**The lane.** It is on top of its problem: its own answer names the same prototype and the same gaps. [read 20] The proof above waits on that lane for two proof blocks and on ours for the audit beneath them. [relayed 20] [read 23] It would be faster and more principled building the attacking server and measuring the cost now, not after that proof. [judgment]

##### 1. What a lab's security engineer wants to see

- **Unit: bytes out a year against the weights' size.** RAND's fourth of five security levels caps all outbound connections together, in hardware, at "e.g., 5 percent" of the weights' size a year. [read 1] Anthropic's ASL-3 standard limits traffic out of the machines holding weights, with no published number. [read 2]
- **Adversary: whoever controls the inference server.** RAND's third level covers insiders, its fourth and fifth states; ASL-3 excludes sophisticated insiders and states. [read 1] [read 2]
- **Channels: responses, then timing.** A large service sends hundreds of gigabytes of responses a day, near the weights' own size, and that channel cannot be capped. [read 3] One paper recomputes sampled responses and holds a compromised server under 0.5% of those bytes, assuming timing carries nothing. [read 4]
- **Test: an attack.** RAND's fourth level places software beside the weights that keeps trying to reach the outside. [read 1]
- OpenAI names "egress controls" (limits on outbound traffic) without numbers; Google DeepMind adopts RAND's levels. [read 5] [read 6]

##### 2. What a lab's performance engineer wants to see

- **One full load (the node's cards fully used), with and without the device:** output tokens a second and time to first token, at the median and the 99th percentile. [read 7] [read 8]
- **The bar is tens of milliseconds:** two gateways (proxies in front of model servers) publish 13 ms added at the 99th percentile and 61 ms added to first token at the median. [read 8]
- **Streaming and TLS still work, and a failure is plain to the client.** [judgment]

##### 3. What the lane has built and shown

- **Demonstrated on a served run.** Ten named attacks, each refused or counted, on Llama-3.2-1B on one H200 with the certifier on a separate machine (Thu 5 Nov). [relayed 9] An accepted audit there (Mon 9 Nov): its proved bound, 446 GB each 128 s execution phase, is too loose, as the lane says. [relayed 11; GB my arithmetic] GLM-5.3 behind the certifier on our eight-H200 node today: 2,240 short connections, none failed, no proof, no attack. [relayed 12]
- **Built, not run on a served model.** Response lengths: the cap, the certifier's signed length records and their proof block reached `main` today; no audit reads them. [run 10] [read 13] Timing inside a tick (when within its 100 ms tick a release leaves): a software test across two of our CPU hosts, with no model. A receiver recovered 0.0064 bit a tick with the server host's cores kept from idling, and 0.024 and 0.054 bit with them free. 300 GB a year allows 0.00017 to 0.00042 bit, so the software certifier is 15 to 38 times over at its best. [relayed 14, 26]
- **Designed.** The proof that a response is the model's output (part 5): one proof block is being written, nothing has run. [relayed 20] Release at a time set in the network card: no machine of ours can. [relayed 14]
- **Not addressed.** TLS ("both sides are plain TCP"). [read 13] Other routes out, beyond a mock datacenter on one host. [read 16] Cost: no run compares with and without. [judgment] Today the certifier held every response a fixed 15 s, against 0.25 s to the server's own first token (median, below a full load); [relayed 12] at 128,000-token prompts the lane expects above 101 s. [relayed 14]

**The lane's table:** the network certifier's part of GLM-5.3's exfiltration capacity, in GB, modeled by the Lean check's counting rule. A datacenter is 12,500 nodes, the world 46.87 million. A stop check is the audit's check that a response ends where the model's stop rule ends it. The two middle rows have no run behind them. [relayed 20]

### 5. The brief, final (same text as the note)

### Which serving rate the 300 GB goal is read at

1. **Decide the rate.** We recommend reading the 300 GB goal at the highest rate at which unmodified vLLM, set up by its own recipe, holds a stated latency bound: not at the assumed utilization (MFU) 0.4, nor at our measured 279.5 tokens a GPU-second.
2. **Decide the run.** That rate takes three to eight hours of our eight-H200 machine: three (our vLLM team lead's guess) for today's settings on our workload; eight (my estimate), which we recommend, add speculative decoding and a public workload.
3. **If yes,** the vLLM lead has offered to book its three-hour run in the first free slot after Thursday morning, on your word or the proofs lead's. The machine's lease ends Sat 14 Nov 12:07 AM PST.

**Why the rate matters.** Exfiltration capacity bounds the data a datacenter could send out past our audit. The goal is 300 GB a year over the world's datacenters. On the same cards and audit budget, it grows in proportion to the tokens served.

#### 1. Our two numbers

**Assumed: utilization 0.4**, with no measurement behind it. Utilization is the share of a card's data-sheet peak that the model's arithmetic uses. On an H200 and our workload it means 4,994 tokens a GPU-second (my arithmetic: 40% of 1,979 TFLOPS, at our count of 159 GFLOP a token).

**Measured: 279.5 tokens a GPU-second**, one 16-minute pass.

- Server: unmodified vLLM 0.28 at its defaults. GLM-5.3 with FP8 weights, one engine tensor-parallel across eight H200s. Prefix caching on, speculative decoding off.
- Workload: 651 requests modeled on production traffic. Short chats, and 47 prompts of 8,000 to 131,000 tokens that hold 95% of the prompt tokens.
- Load: Poisson arrivals at 1.6 requests a second, four times what the server kept up with. No latency bound held: the median request waited 330 seconds for its first token.
- Counted: prompt tokens not served from the cache, 92% of the count, plus output tokens, 22.9 a GPU-second alone.

**The gap.** The run is utilization 2.2%, 18 times below 0.4 (my arithmetic). The nearest public number is SemiAnalysis's, for the predecessor GLM-5 on eight H200s with the SGLang engine, 8,000 tokens in and 1,000 out: 572 to 852 tokens a GPU-second, prompt and output together. So 0.4 is six to nine times above it and our run two to three times below, roughly.

#### 2. What a performance engineer wants to see

- **Metrics.** Throughput at a stated bound on time to first token and time per output token: MLPerf's Server test reports the highest Poisson arrival rate that keeps the 99th percentile of each inside it. Beside it, the rate with no bound, and prompt and output tokens apart.
- **Workload.** Public and named: it moves the rate as much as tuning does. MLPerf uses long documents (mean 9,400 tokens in, 680 out), SemiAnalysis random tokens.
- **Serving configuration.** Engine and version, weight precision, cards per engine, batch limits, prefix caching, speculative decoding, passes, and evidence of tuning: its published recipe, or a sweep.

#### 3. Speculative decoding

A small draft layer (an MTP head) proposes the next few tokens. The full model checks them in one pass and keeps the matches.

- **vLLM** supports it at our version and its current release, and GLM-5.3 ships the layer. vLLM's recipe for GLM-5 on eight H200s turns it on, "for low latency & small batch size".
- **Measured.** Never by us. SemiAnalysis, GLM-5 on H200s, 1,000 tokens in and out: 329 tokens a GPU-second with it, 145 without, both at 41 output tokens a second per user.
- **Who serves with it.** Google says AI Overviews does. SemiAnalysis writes that "most frontier labs" do for DeepSeek's model.
- **Our earlier decision.** On 7 Nov you asked the vLLM team to "either include it or state why it's excluded". It recommended leaving it out: "Nothing on our side can express it today." We found no ruling of yours since.
- **What it touches** (the vLLM team's account; I read only that our code refuses it). The audit recomputes sampled parts of the served computation from a registered circuit of the model. That circuit would need the draft layer and a step that checks several tokens at once. The count of accepted draft tokens must be recomputed, or charged as leakable bits.

#### 4. Options

Each figure is the compute audit's part of the exfiltration capacity once every designed improvement has landed: about 1,120 GB at utilization 0.4 (the proofs lead's; modeled, not built). Other cells scale it by the rate (my arithmetic, except B).

| Rate the goal is read at | What it measures | For and against, from a performance engineer | Exfiltration figure, GB a year (the compute audit's part) | What it takes to run | Main risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Assumed utilization 0.4** (4,994 tokens a GPU-second; not measured) | Nothing. | For: none. Against: no source, and six to nine times the public rates for this model family on these cards. | About 1,120 (the proofs lead's, modeled). For the system as built today it is 29,319, and every figure below is 26 times larger. | Nothing. | We report missing the goal 3.7 times over, at a rate no public benchmark comes near. |
| **B. No latency bound, overloaded, vLLM's defaults** (279.5; measured, one pass) | The most tokens this untuned server computed, whatever the wait: doubling the arrival rate computed no more. The vLLM lead: "a ceiling for one untuned setup, not a production serving rate." | For: a real run, and MLPerf's Offline test is the same idea. Against: still untuned. The bound must grow with the prompt. A rate above 1,340 misses the goal even with every designed improvement. |

**What would change it**

- Batch jobs count too: read the goal at the same server's higher rate with no latency bound.
- No machine hours: quote B and the public range, 63 to 191 GB.
- Speculative decoding adds under a tenth on our workload: leave it out and say so. Much more: add it to the circuit first.

#### 5. What I could not establish

- Who chose 0.4.
- Any rate at which our workload holds a latency bound.
- What limits our server: its cards report 99.9% busy at utilization 2.2%.
- What a top lab's own servers reach. None publish it.
- A tuned configuration. The vLLM lead has none it "would defend to a performance engineer as a tuned production server".

### 2. The id packed at 18 bits

**2.1 The shape** [mine; not built, not run through circuit-check].
- **One unit packs 8 ids.** `IdPack_v1{W=18,N=8}`: parameters `id0` … `id7`, each an `I32` and each one whole output field of one select unit; returns one field `Array<8,Value<18>>`, bit 18j + i of it being bit i of `id_j`. 8 × 18 = 144 bits = 9 words exactly [run: scratch, the verifier's packing gives 9 words; read: `Bits.lean:685-698`, an array is one field]. Wires only on gates: the high 14 bits of each id are read by nothing and returned by nothing, so no lemma about an id's range is needed.
- **A request's return is then 110 such fields** (880 ids, the last 5 zero): 15,840 bits against 28,000, and 15,750 would be the 875 ids alone. "875 ids in 985 words" as one field of one unit (15,760 bits) packs the same way [run: scratch], but one unit cannot gather 875 units' outputs (below).
- **Why not one `Value<18>` a token:** a field is laid on words of its own, so it returns 2 words, 32 bits, the same as today [run: scratch; read: `Bits.lean:698`].
- **The select's `I32` stays inside the replay block**, read by the next step, the stop block's row and the pack unit, and is no longer returned.

**2.2 Against the output-size rule.** A proof block's outputs fit a public size class, a power of two from 16 to 262,144 bits (provisional). The pack unit's 144 bits are in the class of 256: it passes. Under the 16-bit limit (`UNIT_CLASS_MAX` = 16) it does not, and neither does today's select, whose `I32` is 32 bits and whose id cannot fit 16 (V = 154,880): the shape would then be eight units returning each id's low 16 bits and one returning the eight high pairs, the same 9 words [mine].

**2.3 Against how the first stage commits the returned ids.** With one row a token (2 words) the first stage's port matches the select's unit. With the pack unit the returning unit is the pack unit, so the port is **one row for each 8 ids, 9 words wide**. The row's width therefore has to be the returning field's words, not a constant 2: that belongs in the decision the vLLM lane is making now. One thing I could not settle: the stop block and the egress tie read a request's ids as one row (`b.egress`), while a link reads one row a returning unit; whichever layout is picked, the two must be one commitment or tied by a block, or the ids are committed twice with nothing between them [mine].

**2.4 What stops it today.** A pack unit's eight ports all read the select's one output port. Flock's Lean verifier refuses a session in which two ports read one writer port ("two ports of one published frame-v3 domain", `verity/protocols/flock/verifier/Flock/PortRoots.lean:107`, `:133`), which is where the new select's combine stops [relayed: the 19:39Z entry, stop 5, run `r20261111-192333-4ab8`]. **So the pack unit lands behind whichever way out is taken for the new select**, and adds no new obstacle of its own [guess]. If that refusal stays, a chain does the same packing with one unit a token, each reading its select and the previous unit's carry (two different writer ports), at the price of eight more templates in the second stage's sample [mine; not costed].

|---|---:|---:|

- **Should a figure carry it: yes, beside the bound, never inside it** [mine; a recommendation].

## STOPS, Wed 11 Nov 20:19Z: your two answers for PRF-477. The Lean run takes one coin evidence a stage and never compares the two, so one session over both stages and two sessions on two roots both pass it, and both ran. The auditor's parameters are a function of the class's layout and the replay sample's size; #8875 holds the function and no command that runs it before the sample

The form's switch on, ahead of its proof; not `main`'s verifier, for every run named. Line numbers are on `main` at `61f13c2275fb`, and at #8875's head `092004fadea9` for `two_stage.py`.

**1. The interior commitment's session.**

- **Does the Lean run read two sessions?** It reads one piece of coin evidence a stage [read]. `Spot.Run.run` takes `Input.coins` for the first stage (`Spot/Run.lean:113`, checked at `:259`) and `Interior.coins` for the second (`:85`, checked at `:201`); `Stream.outcome` hands them as `coins` and `interior_coins` (`service.py:2257-2260`, docstring `:2285-2286`). Each goes through `coinsHold` (`:161`) to `Challenger.coinsReason` (`Spot/ChallengerCoins.lean:105`) with that stage's own registration: the evidence `{key, ledger, main, pins, segment, session}` must show the bytes the sample read to be exactly the coins that the one session the auditor's ledger opens for that registration's window root released after that registration's digest, consecutive and every one read (`trustedSessionOf`, `Spot/ChallengerSession.lean:906`; `challengerStream`, `readReason`, `ChallengerCoins.lean:56`, `:77`). The root is the params' `windowRoot`, what `register` and `register_interiors` were given as `window_root`. The session must have withheld its commitment (`withheldOn`, `:95`), been closed by its client, and run a commit on `main`'s first-parent line [read].
- **What it checks about their order in the challenger's log.** Inside each session's release log, that the coins are the ones released after the registration's digest; between the two sessions, nothing [read]. Nothing in `Run.lean` reads one evidence's ledger, session or log against the other's, so there is no check that the interior's session opened after the boundary's closed, or that the two are in one ledger. What orders the stages is the records: the second stage's coins follow the interior registration's digest; the interior record names the first stage's sample, which the check of the statements holds to the verifier's own (`second-interior-order`, `SecondStage.lean:1029`, `:1048`); and the interior registration's R1 to R8 run against the interior's own copies (`Run.lean:196`), which `register_interiors` describes as the log whose last record is the registration it follows (`service.py:2057`) [read].

### 1. The statement

```lean
-- the escape a verification phase's strategy fixes: P̄_a at the boundary values' footprint at best interiors
noncomputable def escAt (L : CompiledTwo Coin A) (x : Msg) (val : ℕ → Option Bool) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  match L.parse x with
  | none => 1
  | some s =>
    match L.partition s, L.two s with
    | some Pt, some d => if InScopeTwo Pt d s then ENNReal.ofReal (d.PaBestAt s Pt val) else 1
    | _, _ => 1

-- the event's probability: the run accepts and its sample holds a proof block incorrect at `val` and the committed interiors
noncomputable def acceptedSampledAt (H : Msg → Msg) (L : CompiledTwo Coin A) (x : Msg) (P : Prover Unit)
    (val : ℕ → Option Bool) : ℝ :=
  Pr fun r : Fin (L.V.k x) → Coin =>
    (run H P L.V x () r).out = .acc ∧ ∃ u ∈ L.checked x r, u ∈ L.FregTwoAt H P x () val r

def PeriodTwoProd (H : Msg → Msg) (Lv : ℕ → CompiledTwo Coin A)
    (val : (t : ℕ) → Msg → Prover Unit → ℕ → Option Bool) : Prop :=
  ∀ (T : ℕ) (ε : ℕ → ℝ) (s : Strategy (periodG (fun t => twoGame (Lv t) ((O → V) × Tick × Adv)) 0 T)),
    (∀ t τ, PeriodPlays (fun t => twoGame (Lv t) ((O → V) × Tick × Adv)) 0 T s t τ → (Lv t).Scope τ.2.1.1 →
      acceptedSampledAt H (Lv t) τ.2.1.1 τ.2.1.2 (val t τ.2.1.1 τ.2.1.2) ≤ ε t) →
    ∀ δ : ℝ, Verity.Game.value
        (fun l : List (ServedEsc O V Tick Adv) =>
          (∀ r ∈ l, r.accepted) ∧ (l.map ServedEsc.escape).prod < ENNReal.ofReal δ)
        (twoAtRun H Lv val T s) ≤
      ENNReal.ofReal δ + ∑ t ∈ Finset.range T, ENNReal.ofReal (ε t)

-- the theorem: the two-stage contract at every phase, and nothing else
theorem periodTwoProd_of (H : Msg → Msg) (Lv : ℕ → CompiledTwo Coin A)
    (val : (t : ℕ) → Msg → Prover Unit → ℕ → Option Bool) (hS : ∀ t, (Lv t).Sessions H) :
    PeriodTwoProd H Lv val
```

What the names are [read, my file]: `twoGame` is `main`'s verification phase (`Proofs/WeightSecurity/Two.lean:49`: the datacenter sends the release, then the statement `x` and a prover `P` with no tape, then the verifier flips all of the run's coins); `τ.2.1.1` and `τ.2.1.2` are that `x` and `P`. `val t x P` is the boundary trace read at phase `t`, a parameter. `FregTwoAt` is `main`'s `FregTwo` with the boundary values a parameter (the interiors are the committed ones, `iregVal`). `twoAtRun` records each phase as a `Served` plus one field, `escape := escAt (Lv t) x (val t x P)`. `PaBestAt` is `Design.Two.Pa` at `val`'s footprint at interiors that maximize each replay block's escape; the proof file shows every such interiors give one number (`Design.Two.paBestAt_eq`).

**In plain words.** Take a period of T verification phases of the two-stage design, played by one adversary that may choose each phase's statement and prover after seeing every earlier phase's coins. Suppose that in each phase, on a statement in scope, the probability that the run is accepted while its sample holds a proof block that is wrong at the boundary trace is at most ε_t. Then, for every δ, the probability that every phase is accepted and the phases' acceptance probabilities P̄_a (each at its boundary trace's footprint, at the interiors most favourable to the prover) multiply to less than δ is at most δ + Σ_t ε_t. The sampling term is δ once, however many phases the period has.

### 3. Does the 19:40Z entry's reading hold? Yes, at best interiors, and only there

`period_prod` (`Proofs/Flock/EndToEnd/Joint/Prod.lean:28`) asks, at each strategy τ that plays a phase: one finite number `e` that every outcome's record carries (`∀ b, esc (rec i τ b) = e`), with the phase's miss probability at most `e` [read]. Both hold [guess until the run: by reading]:
- **Fixed before the coins.** In `twoGame` the strategy has sent `x` and `P` before any coin of the run, and `P` has no tape. `escAt (Lv t) x (val t x P)` reads `x` and `val t x P` only. At `main`'s trace `regVal H P x ()` is the value the extractions open most often over the run's and the extractor's coins, a function of `x` and `P`.
- **It bounds the miss.** `CompiledTwo.pr_missTwo_le_Pa` (`TwoRegMiss.lean:138`) at the tape `()`: over all of the run's coins, the sample holds no proof block incorrect at `val` and the committed interiors with probability at most `P̄_a` at `val`'s footprint at best interiors. It takes the contract only.
- **Why "at best interiors" is forced.** The committed interiors (`iregVal`) read the first stage's coins, so the footprint at the committed interiors is not fixed by τ and `period_prod` cannot take it. The footprint at best interiors is, and it bounds the other cell by cell (`pr_missTwo_fork_le`, `TwoRegMiss.lean:112`). So the product that multiplies is of `P̄_a` at the boundary trace's footprint **at the interiors most favourable to the prover**, which is what `KSRegTwo` and `HeadlineTwo` already read for one phase.
- **The one condition.** The boundary trace must be a function of the phase's statement and prover. `regVal` at the tape `Unit` and `regValX` are; a trace that read the run's coins would not be.

### 4. What it does not give

1. **Not what is served** [read]. `escAt` reads `val`, the trace the extractions open, a definition of the proof. Nothing here ties it to the released bytes. That is piece (3).
2. **Not a count or a number of bits.** The conclusion is "the phases' `P̄_a` multiply to at least δ". Turning that into "at most K incorrect replay blocks, or B bits, over the period" is piece (2). One consequence is immediate from `main`'s `Design.Two.Pa_le_pow` (`TwoCap.lean:96`): at rates `r₁`, `r₂` each `P̄_a ≤ (1 − r₁r₂)^{n_t}`, `n_t` the replay blocks wrong at phase t's boundary, so Σ_t n_t ≤ ln(1/δ)/ln(1/(1 − r₁r₂)). That is `compilerPeriodTwoReg`'s shape again, no better; the gain the cost model counts on is in weighing each cell at its own rate, which is piece (2) [guess, not written].
3. **Nothing about a run in which a phase is rejected.** "Every phase accepted" is `JointStratifiedHorizon`'s event, and what you asked for. But the datacenter releases before each verdict and halts only after a rejection, so an adversary willing to be caught in phase k has already released phases 1 to k − 1, and this statement is silent on that run. Section 5 has the form that is not.
4. **Σ_t ε_t grows with T.** At a verification phase of 600 s a year has 52,560 phases, so the event's term costs log₂ 52,560 = 15.7 bits against one phase's ε over a year, 12.1 over a month, 10.0 over a week [run, python]. With `main`'s per-phase 2^-95.87 that is 2^-80.2 over a year [modeled from my 19:56Z figure, not a Lean statement].
5. **The design is not judged.** A statement whose design samples nothing has `P̄_a = 1` and the conclusion says nothing; the rates enter where the product is turned into a count.
6. **Strictness.** It bounds "product < δ", so outside it the product is ≥ δ; `M̄_δ` on `main` is `δ < P̄_a`. Same as `JointStratifiedHorizon`. The non-strict form follows by a limit and is not written.

### 5. The form a capacity figure needs, one step past what was asked

```lean
-- the escapes of the phases before the first whose sample holds an incorrect proof block, multiplied
noncomputable def ServedEsc.leadEscape : List (ServedEsc O V Tick Adv) → ℝ≥0∞
  | [] => 1
  | w :: l => if w.sampledIncorrect then 1 else w.escape * leadEscape l

def ServedEsc.UndetectedBelow (δ : ℝ) (l : List (ServedEsc O V Tick Adv)) : Prop :=
  (∃ w ∈ l, w.accepted ∧ w.sampledIncorrect) ∨ leadEscape l < ENNReal.ofReal δ

def PeriodTwoLead (H) (Lv) (val) : Prop :=
  ∀ T ε s, (the same hypothesis on the event) →
    ∀ δ : ℝ, Verity.Game.value (ServedEsc.UndetectedBelow δ) (twoAtRun H Lv val T s) ≤
      ENNReal.ofReal δ + ∑ t ∈ Finset.range T, ENNReal.ofReal (ε t)
```

In plain words: except with probability δ + Σ_t ε_t, no accepted phase's sample holds a proof block wrong at its boundary trace, and the phases **before the first phase whose sample does hold one** have `P̄_a` that multiply to at least δ, whatever happens after. It is `PeriodTwoReg` (`Served.Undetected`, `Served.lead`) with the escapes multiplied in place of one rate raised to a count; it implies `PeriodTwoProd`; and its premises are the same.     Finset ((t : Fin n) → Finset ℕ) :=
  (Fintype.piFinset fun t => (Finset.range (Pt t).blocks.length).powerset).filter fun T =>
    δ ≤ ∏ t, (d t).Pa (Pt t) (counts (Pt t) (d t).part (T t))

def AdmissiblePeriodTwoRankin : Prop :=
  ∀ (n : ℕ) (s : Fin n → AuditStatement) (Pt : Fin n → Partition) (d : Fin n → Design.Two)
    (q : Fin n → ℕ → ℝ) (δ θ : ℝ), (∀ t, InScopeTwo (Pt t) (d t) (s t)) →

        δ ^ (-θ) * ∏ t, ∏ ρ ∈ Finset.range (d t).part.blocks.length,

def servedAt (s : AuditStatement) (val : ℕ → Option Bool) : Fin s.prog.outs.length → Bool :=
  fun i => (s.prog.read val s.prog.outs[i]).getD false
def inputsAt (s : AuditStatement) (val : ℕ → Option Bool) (g : ℕ) : Option Bool :=
  if s.prog.gates[g]? = some .input then val g else none

/-- What a period can serve at inputs a: the outputs of every family of boundary traces with those inputs
whose phases' P̄_a, at their footprints at some interiors, multiply to at least δ. -/

    (∀ t, inputsAt (s t) (val t) = a t) ∧
    (∃ ι : (t : Fin n) → ℕ → ℕ → Bool,
      δ ≤ ∏ t, (d t).Pa (Pt t) (footprintAt (s t) (Pt t) (d t).part (val t) (ι t))) ∧
    ∀ t, servedAt (s t) (val t) = y t

```

**What our own plan's lengths were modeled on: no source stated.** `prefix_plan.py` only copies lengths and arrival gaps out of the serve plan [read whole]. The plan's meta file (`ctx128k_plan.meta.json` of that artifact, fetched now with `research data fetch`) names its parts and no outside source for the mix: 482 ShareGPT requests (largest prompt 1,015), 122 multi-turn requests (largest 1,775), 29 "long" (largest 32,278), 16 "long128k" (largest 130,808) and 2 follow-ups; the long prompts are 16 Project Gutenberg books each followed by a request to summarize the book; 0.4 requests a second for 1,500 s, seed 0; and the long requests were held to a budget of 330,000 tokens out of 370,000, with a model of the server recording that nothing is preempted [read whole: the meta file's fields, no row]. A reader would be right to call that mix ours: it was sized to our server.

**MLPerf's latency limits, for each LLM benchmark** (Server scenario: Poisson arrivals, the result is the highest arrival rate at which 99% of requests stay inside both limits; no reuse of work across requests is allowed, so no prefix caching) [read whole: `inference_rules.adoc` in mlcommons/inference_policies]:

- Llama3.1-405B, the long-context one (prompts up to 20,000 tokens): first token within 6,000 ms and 175 ms per output token; Interactive 4,500 ms and 80 ms.
- Llama2-70B (prompts up to 1,024): 2,000 ms and 200 ms; Interactive 450 ms and 40 ms. Llama3.1-8B (up to 2,048): 2,000 ms and 100 ms; Interactive 500 ms and 30 ms. Mixtral-8x7B: 2,000 ms and 200 ms.
- DeepSeek-R1 (up to 3,136): 2,000 ms and 80 ms; Interactive 1,500 ms and 15 ms. GPT-OSS-120B (up to 15,330): 3,000 ms and 80 ms; Interactive 2,000 ms and 20 ms. Speculative decoding is allowed only in those two Interactive benchmarks and one edge benchmark.

**vLLM's own client at our pin** [read whole: `docs/benchmarking/cli.md` and `sweeps.md`; excerpt: `datasets.py`, `serve.py`]:

- `--dataset-name` takes `sharegpt`, `burstgpt`, `sonnet`, `random`, `random-mm`, `random-rerank`, `hf`, `custom`, `custom_audio`, `custom_image`, `prefix_repetition`, `spec_bench`, `speed_bench`, `timed_trace`; the default is `random`.
- Long prompts come from `timed_trace` (somebody else's table), `speed_bench` (up to 32,000), `hf` with MLPerf's set (up to 19,970), and `random`, `prefix_repetition` or `custom` at any length we choose.
- `timed_trace` sends a table made by someone else: JSON lines of arrival time, prompt length, output length and block ids, with the field names and block size set by flags. It builds each prompt from random tokens seeded by its block ids, so repeated blocks hit the prefix cache. With `--no-self-timed` it ignores the table's arrival times and sends the same requests at `--request-rate`.
- It sweeps: `--request-rate` gives Poisson arrivals (or burstier with `--burstiness`), `--max-concurrency` holds a number in flight, and `vllm bench sweep serve_workload` steps through arrival rates or numbers in flight. `--goodput` reports the requests a second that met stated limits at the rate run; it does not search for the highest such rate.
- The same page says these benchmarks are "mainly for evaluating specific vLLM features as well as regression testing" and recommends GuideLLM for benchmarking a live server. GuideLLM [read whole: README and trace guide; excerpt: its profiles' sources] reads Moonshot's format (`kind=mooncake`), the AgentX format (`kind=weka`) and a plain table of times and lengths, steps through rates (`sweep`), and has a profile that searches for the highest load inside latency limits (`goodput`).

**Where I looked and found nothing.**

- A trace published by OpenAI, Anthropic or Google of their own API traffic: none found. OpenRouter's study gives averages and no file [excerpt]; LMSYS-Chat-1M and WildChat hold short chat text with no arrival times [memory].
- An outside benchmark that sweeps a grid of fixed prompt lengths above 32,000 to a peak rate under a latency limit: none found. The 100,000-token cells that exist (GuideLLM's, Artificial Analysis's, SPEED-Bench's) come with no latency limit, and MLPerf's limits stop at 20,000-token prompts.
- A loader for the Copilot or FreeInference traces in vLLM's client, GuideLLM or AIPerf: none in their dataset lists [excerpt].
- Also seen and not used: Alibaba's ServeGen (NSDI '26) is a generator fitted to Alibaba's traffic, not a trace, and its README gives no lengths [read whole]; `thangquang09/agentic-coding-traces` is synthetic [excerpt]. One web search and the dataset lists of GuideLLM's and AIPerf's docs were my only finding aids, so a trace neither names could be missed.

**Recommendation.**

1. Name **Moonshot AI's conversation trace and tool-and-agent trace** as the traffic, sent by `vllm bench serve` with the command on vLLM's own page. Keep each trace's lengths and repeated blocks, step the arrival rate (`--no-self-timed --request-rate`, as MLPerf does with its fixed set), and report the highest rate that keeps MLPerf's long-context limits (first token in 6 s, 175 ms per output token, 99% of requests). Then neither the traffic, the client nor the limit is ours.
2. Beside it report **a grid with no mix to pick**, each cell an outside scenario: 1,000/1,000, 8,000/1,000 and 100,000/1,000 prompt/output tokens (GuideLLM's built-in cells; 8,192/1,024 is also InferenceX's one fixed cell, and 100,000 is Artificial Analysis's longest). Step each cell to its peak, print every cell, and evaluate the bound at the 100,000-token cell. No outside benchmark can be adopted whole: the cells are theirs, the stepping rule is MLPerf's.
3. For "what a lab sees", **cite Microsoft's GitHub Copilot trace as the evidence** that such traffic is long and repeats itself (median prompt 56,826 tokens, 93% of prompt tokens in prompts over 32,000, 86% served from cache), and say plainly that no vLLM client sends it as it is. Sending it needs a converter we would write and a tenth of its calls do not fit our model, so that run would be partly ours; I would leave it for a follow-up.
4. The paper must say three things about any of these traces: they hold lengths, times and block ids and never text, so every prompt is random tokens; Moonshot's hour is one Chinese chat service, recorded before its February 2025 release, with arrival times rounded to 3-second marks; and speculative decoding cannot be judged on random tokens (SPEED-Bench is the outside real-text set for that).
5. Keep our 651-request plan out of the headline. If it appears, label it ours, with "no source stated" for its mix.

**Read whole, and not.**

- Read whole now: Azure's readmes for 2023, 2024 and the Copilot traces, with the Copilot dataset card and schema; BurstGPT's README; MLPerf's rules file and the 405B benchmark's README; vLLM's `docs/benchmarking/cli.md`, `sweeps.md` and `serving-tests.json` at our pin; the Moonshot release's README; Bailian's README; InferenceX's README, its end-to-end README, `agentx-standalone.md`, `CONFIGS.md` and `PRINCIPLES.md`; both AgentX dataset cards; GuideLLM's README, trace guide and seven scenario files; FreeInference's dataset card; Artificial Analysis's method page; ServeGen's README; our `prefix_plan.py`, `prefix_plan.source.json` and the plan's meta file.
- Computed over every row now: every data file in the table, among them all seven days of the Copilot traces and all sixteen weeks of FreeInference's request tables.
- Read only in part: vLLM's `datasets.py` and `serve.py` (the loaders and the flags); InferenceX's `MODELS.md` and client code; GuideLLM's other guides and sources; the SPEED-Bench card and TraceLab's README (the middle of each); AIPerf's README and tutorials; OpenRouter's study (two sections). Of the papers I read only the Copilot paper's abstract.
- Not tried: I sent nothing to a server, so "can send it as it is" rests on reading the loaders and vLLM's own example, not on a run.

Yes: Moonshot AI's published hour of its Kimi service's traffic has prompts up to 126,195 tokens (a third of its prompt tokens sit in prompts over 32,000) and is the very file vLLM's own benchmark page replays, and an outside long-context benchmark, OpenDC-Infer-LC, already pairs that trace with a grid of fixed prompt lengths and latency limits; four newer coding-agent traces are far longer (GitHub Copilot's median prompt is 56,826 tokens), but no vLLM client sends those as they are.

From SERVERATE (`bc-c5a8af69-8dc6-54b5-9a8f-c38a7d955296`). This entry is the final one and stands on its own; it replaces my first entry of 20:58Z. What changed since then: four more rows (the Chutes trace, the SwissAI trace, the OpenDC-Infer-LC benchmark, an IETF draft), a warning about vLLM's client at long prompts, and recommendation 2, which now adopts an outside grid instead of one I assembled. Every time is from `date -u`. I ran nothing on a GPU and booked nothing.

**The answer in five points.**

1. A published record of real traffic with long prompts, made by somebody else, that `vllm bench serve` sends as it is: **Moonshot AI's conversation trace and its tool-and-agent trace** (the FAST '25 release in the Mooncake repository). vLLM's benchmark page at our pin uses that conversation file as its worked example of `--dataset-name timed_trace` [read whole: `docs/benchmarking/cli.md` at `d9105ea800`]. Every request of both files fits the 131,072-token limit our own long-context plan was made for (largest prompt plus output 126,527) [computed from the file; the limit read from our plan's meta file].
2. The traffic a lab's coding product sees is now published four times over, and it is much longer: Microsoft's sample of GitHub Copilot's agent (9.3 million calls in a week), Harvard's FreeInference trace, the University of Washington's TraceLab and SemiAnalysis's AgentX corpus. Their median prompts are 56,826 to 142,016 tokens [computed from the files]. None is in the form `vllm bench serve` reads (one request a line, with block ids), and a fifth to two thirds of their calls are over 100,000 tokens [computed from the files].
3. The older, most-cited traces have no long prompts at all: Azure 2023 and 2024 (largest 14,050; the 2024 week has none over 8,000) and BurstGPT's first two files (largest 31,407). MLPerf's long-context benchmark stops at 19,970 tokens [computed from the files].
4. vLLM's own standing serving tests are short: ShareGPT and random tokens of 128 or 2,048 in and out [read whole: `.buildkite/performance-benchmarks/tests/serving-tests.json` at our pin]. So "vLLM's standard suite" alone has no long context; "the trace vLLM's own page replays" does.
5. A grid we could adopt as it is exists: **OpenDC-Infer-LC** (Maincode, EMNLP 2026 Industry Track) fixes prompts of 8,192, 32,768 and 131,072 tokens, steps each to the highest load inside stated latency limits, and takes its real-traffic arrival times and length mix from Moonshot's conversation trace [excerpt: the paper; read whole: its workload config]. It is new: its repository was created 29 Aug 2026 and has no stars [read: GitHub]. On its authors' own server no arrival rate kept the limits under the trace's mix [excerpt: the paper's section 4.3], which is a warning for us too.

**How to read the table.** Lengths are tokens. A tag at the end of a cell covers every fact in that cell: [read whole] I read the whole page or file now; [computed from the file] I downloaded the data file now and computed over every row (percentiles are nearest-rank; the Chutes row says which part of that file I read); [excerpt] I read only part; [memory] not checked now. "Share over 8,000 / 32,000" is the share of all prompt tokens (or output tokens) that sit in prompts (or outputs) longer than that. "vLLM's client" is `vllm bench serve` at our pin `0.28.1rc1.dev472+gd9105ea80`.

The plan's meta file (`ctx128k_plan.meta.json` of that artifact, fetched now with `research data fetch`) names its parts and no outside source for the mix: 482 ShareGPT requests (largest prompt 1,015), 122 multi-turn requests (largest 1,775), 29 "long" (largest 32,278), 16 "long128k" (largest 130,808) and 2 follow-ups; the long prompts are 16 Project Gutenberg books each followed by a request to summarize the book; 0.4 requests a second for 1,500 s, seed 0; and the long requests were held to a budget of 330,000 tokens out of 370,000, with a model of the server recording that nothing is preempted [read whole: the meta file's fields, no row]. A reader would be right to call that mix ours: it was sized to our server.

**MLPerf's latency limits, for each LLM benchmark** (Server scenario: Poisson arrivals, the result is the highest arrival rate at which 99% of requests stay inside both limits; no reuse of work across requests is allowed, so no prefix caching) [read whole: `inference_rules.adoc` in mlcommons/inference_policies]:

- Llama3.1-405B, the long-context one (prompts up to 20,000 tokens): first token within 6,000 ms and 175 ms per output token; Interactive 4,500 ms and 80 ms.
- Llama2-70B (prompts up to 1,024): 2,000 ms and 200 ms; Interactive 450 ms and 40 ms. Llama3.1-8B (up to 2,048): 2,000 ms and 100 ms; Interactive 500 ms and 30 ms. Mixtral-8x7B: 2,000 ms and 200 ms.
- DeepSeek-R1 (up to 3,136): 2,000 ms and 80 ms; Interactive 1,500 ms and 15 ms. GPT-OSS-120B (up to 15,330): 3,000 ms and 80 ms; Interactive 2,000 ms and 20 ms. Speculative decoding is allowed only in those two Interactive benchmarks and one edge benchmark.

**vLLM's own client at our pin** [read whole: `docs/benchmarking/cli.md` and `sweeps.md`; excerpt: `datasets.py`, `serve.py`]:

- `--dataset-name` takes `sharegpt`, `burstgpt`, `sonnet`, `random`, `random-mm`, `random-rerank`, `hf`, `custom`, `custom_audio`, `custom_image`, `prefix_repetition`, `spec_bench`, `speed_bench`, `timed_trace`; the default is `random`.
- Long prompts come from `timed_trace` (somebody else's table), `speed_bench` (up to 32,000), `hf` with MLPerf's set (up to 19,970), and `random`, `prefix_repetition` or `custom` at any length we choose.
- `timed_trace` sends a table made by someone else: JSON lines of arrival time, prompt length, output length and block ids, with the field names and block size set by flags. It builds each prompt from random tokens seeded by its block ids, so repeated blocks hit the prefix cache. With `--no-self-timed` it ignores the table's arrival times and sends the same requests at `--request-rate`.
- It sweeps: `--request-rate` gives Poisson arrivals (or burstier with `--burstiness`), `--max-concurrency` holds a number in flight, and `vllm bench sweep serve_workload` steps through arrival rates or numbers in flight. `--goodput` reports the requests a second that met stated limits at the rate run; it does not search for the highest such rate.
- The same page says these benchmarks are "mainly for evaluating specific vLLM features as well as regression testing" and recommends GuideLLM for benchmarking a live server. GuideLLM [read whole: README and trace guide; excerpt: its profiles' sources] reads Moonshot's format (`kind=mooncake`), the AgentX format (`kind=weka`) and a plain table of times and lengths, steps through rates (`sweep`), and has a profile that searches for the highest load inside latency limits (`goodput`).

**A warning about vLLM's client at long prompts.** vLLM issue 39963 (opened 16 Apr 2026, closed unanswered as stale on 17 Aug 2026) reports that `vllm bench serve` showed about a tenth of another client's throughput, and first-token times of minutes, at prompts of 50,000 and 100,000 tokens with many requests in flight, against the same server; the reporter blames the client's read buffer [read whole: the issue]. Our pin's client sets no such buffer [excerpt: `serve.py`]. I did not test it. Before a long-prompt number from vLLM's client goes in the paper, check it once against the server's own counters or a second client.

**Where I looked and found nothing.**

- A trace published by OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Together, Fireworks or Baseten of their own API traffic: none found in three web searches. OpenRouter's study gives averages and no file [excerpt]; LMSYS-Chat-1M and WildChat hold short chat text with no arrival times [memory].
- A well-known benchmark that steps fixed prompt lengths above 32,000 to a peak load under a latency limit: none found. OpenDC-Infer-LC does exactly that but is new. The 100,000-token cells of GuideLLM, Artificial Analysis and SPEED-Bench come with no latency limit, and MLPerf's limits stop at 20,000-token prompts.
- A loader for the Copilot or FreeInference traces in vLLM's client, GuideLLM or AIPerf: none in their dataset lists [excerpt].
- Also seen and not used: Alibaba's ServeGen (NSDI '26) is a generator fitted to Alibaba's traffic, not a trace, and its README gives no lengths [read whole]; `thangquang09/agentic-coding-traces` is synthetic [excerpt]. Three web searches and the dataset lists of GuideLLM's and AIPerf's docs were my only finding aids, so a trace none of them names could be missed.

**Recommendation.**

1. **Traffic:** name Moonshot AI's conversation trace and tool-and-agent trace, sent by `vllm bench serve` with the command on vLLM's own page, keeping each trace's lengths and repeated blocks and stepping the arrival rate (`--no-self-timed --request-rate`). Traffic and client are then somebody else's. For "what a lab sees", cite Microsoft's GitHub Copilot trace as the evidence that such traffic is long and repeats itself (median prompt 56,826 tokens, 86% of prompt tokens served from cache), and say that no vLLM client sends it as it is.
2. **The limit for that run: fix it before running.** MLPerf's long-context limit (first token in 6 s, 175 ms per output token, 99% of requests) is the best known, but it was set for prompts up to 20,000 tokens, and one in a hundred of the conversation trace's prompts is 85,401 tokens or longer. OpenDC-Infer-LC's limits are the only published ones I found that were set for 131,072-token prompts (first token in 10 s). Its authors found no arrival rate inside their limits under this trace's mix, so decide beforehand what we print if we find none either: latency by prompt length at stated rates.
3. **Grid, beside the trace:** OpenDC-Infer-LC's as it is, run with its own client, which leaves no mix to pick: 8,192/512, 32,768/512, 131,072/1,024 and the repeated-prefix cell, each with its own limits, each stepped to its peak, every cell printed, the bound evaluated at the largest cell. Say that the benchmark is new. Its largest cell needs a 135,168-token limit; if our model cannot take that, the largest cell adopted unchanged is 32,768, and anything longer (GuideLLM's 100,000/1,000, say) is a pairing we made.
4. **The paper must say:** the traces hold lengths, times and block ids and never text, so every prompt is random tokens; Moonshot's hour is one Chinese chat service, recorded before its February 2025 release, with arrival times rounded to 3-second marks; and speculative decoding cannot be judged on random tokens (SPEED-Bench is the outside real-text set for that).
5. **Keep our 651-request plan out of the headline;** if it appears, label it ours, with "no source stated" for its mix. Check vLLM's client against the server's own counters at long prompts before trusting it there.

**Read whole, and not.**

- Read whole now: Azure's readmes for 2023, 2024 and the Copilot traces, with the Copilot dataset card and schema; BurstGPT's README; MLPerf's rules file and the 405B benchmark's README; vLLM's `docs/benchmarking/cli.md`, `sweeps.md` and `serving-tests.json` at our pin; the Moonshot release's README; Bailian's README; InferenceX's README, its end-to-end README, `agentx-standalone.md`, `CONFIGS.md` and `PRINCIPLES.md`; both AgentX dataset cards; GuideLLM's README, trace guide and seven scenario files; FreeInference's dataset card; Artificial Analysis's method page; ServeGen's README; the Chutes trace's README; OpenDC-Infer-LC's `configs/datasets.yaml`; vLLM issue 39963; our `prefix_plan.py`, `prefix_plan.source.json` and the plan's meta file.
- Computed over every row now: every data file in the table, among them all seven days of the Copilot traces and all sixteen weeks of FreeInference's request tables. The one exception is the Chutes trace, of which I read 61 of 6,114 row groups, evenly spaced.
- Read only in part: vLLM's `datasets.py` and `serve.py` (the loaders and the flags); InferenceX's `MODELS.md` and client code; GuideLLM's other guides and sources; the SPEED-Bench card and TraceLab's README (the middle of each); AIPerf's README and tutorials; OpenRouter's study (two sections); the OpenDC-Infer-LC paper (its method, section 4.3 and tables 5 and 6), its README (most of it) and its source files (a search for a trace replay); the IETF draft (its workload and long-context sections). Of the traces' papers I read only the Copilot paper's abstract.
- Not tried: I sent nothing to a server, so "can send it as it is" rests on reading the loaders and vLLM's own example, not on a run.

## WIRES, Wed 11 Nov 21:27Z: neither grouping dominates. Tables a session is a dial: each doubling halves the sets of live coins through the ZK server and costs one bit of the binding error; one session a template is out of reach at a datacenter (125,570 tables against the 200 Flock's zero-knowledge scope takes). Pick: several tables a session first, then several sessions a template by groups fixed before the coins

**For Daniel (six lines).** Every count is modeled, none is a run of the served engine.

1. **The tables are fixed; only their grouping is a choice.** A Flock table holds at most 2^35 bits: 256 proof blocks of 2^27 bits up to 32,768 of 2^20 [read, derived]. A datacenter's 600-second verification phase needs about 155,000 to 181,000 tables, 125,570 of them for one subcircuit template [relayed].
2. **Two groupings, and they compose.** (a) Several sessions for a template, one table each: what the quoted figures price. (b) One session of several tables: the one-stage verifier takes it, the second stage refuses it [read]. A template with several sessions of J tables each is both.
3. **Sets of live coins through the ZK server in 600 s.** One table a session: 154,869 to 180,897, one every 3.9 ms if one at a time. 200 tables a session: about 780 to 1,100, one every 0.6 s. ### A. To paste on PRF-548: the interface of the kept verifier, `verify-members`

On `cursor/proofs-keptverify-604f` at `0963ff842e` (the first pull request, not opened). The second pull request (`cursor/proofs-keptcircuit-7c1e` at `5e87ff2c83`, not opened) keeps the last member's circuit file too and changes no line of this.

**Unchanged since Wed 11 Nov 17:56Z**
1. **Start, once a run:** `flock-verify verify-members [--archive DIR] --program F`. `F` is the registered program as `verify` takes `--program`: a path, or with `--archive DIR` its SHA-512 in that archive.
2. **A member:** one line on standard input, a JSON array of strings: `verify`'s argument list for that member, every word after `verify`, its own `--archive`, `--program`, `--partition`, `--registered`, `--zk` and `--session DIR...` among them.
3. **Its answer, on standard output:** the `VERDICT` lines `verify` prints for that member alone, byte for byte, then `MEMBER {"exit":E,"index":I}`, then a flush. `E` is `verify`'s exit status on that list (0 every session accepted, 1 one refused or an exception, 2 stopped before any session). A line that is no argument list gets `MEMBER {"error":WHY,"exit":2,"index":I}`.
4. **One member at a time:** the next line is read only after the last `MEMBER` line is flushed.
5. **Refused:** a session whose `VERDICT` says so; a session of an answered member with no `VERDICT` line of its own; every session of a member with no `MEMBER` line.
6. **The process's exit status:** 0 when every member's is 0, else 1; 2 with nothing printed when it has no program it can read.

**Added since, each held by a test** [run: `r20261111-211945-ca3f`, 5 passed, 0 skipped, on a build of this head]
7. **Standard error:** everything `verify` writes there for a member is written and flushed before that member's `MEMBER` line. A caller that writes a member's line only once the one before it is answered finds, at each `MEMBER` line, that member's lines last and nothing after them. The test splits the file where each `MEMBER` line arrives and holds each piece to what `verify` writes alone, but for the milliseconds.
8. **Files held by content:** `--archive DIR` and a SHA-512 key for the program on the command line; in each line the member's own `--archive` and a key for its circuit, public file, partition and program. The test hands five members, each with an archive of its own.
9. **It opens no connection and writes no file.** It reads standard input, its program and the files its lines name, and writes its two streams. The test runs the whole process, from its start through three members to its end, under a system-call filter that kills it at its first `socket` call; each member is answered as `verify` answers it alone. The condition, in soundness's words: nothing of member k+1 is in the challenger's log before member k's closing `tree-open` round: no coin of k+1 and no line that opens its session.

### 3. The decision on what is served, in three sentences (for tonight's report)

1. **What is missing.** Every bound proved for the two-stage design, on `main` and on my branch, is about the trace the datacenter committed to, while a figure in gigabytes is about the bytes that left the datacenter; to get from one to the other something must say that what an accepted verification phase released is that trace's values at the circuit's outputs, and for the two-stage design `main` neither assumes this, nor has the verifier check it, nor proves it.
2. **The options.** (A) Take it as a hypothesis of the period's bound, as the weight-security guarantees on `main` do today, which is about 100 lines and leaves every gigabyte figure resting on an unproved claim about what a cheating datacenter releases; (B) have the two-stage verifier enforce it against the release the datacenter declares, by putting the release in the statement and holding each sampled proof block's output values to it, so that an output that differs from the release is an incorrect proof block, sampled and counted like any other; or (C) the same check against the network certifier's record of every byte that left, which is the auditor's own device and is how the one-stage design gets it.
3. **My pick is (C).** Only the device's record says what left rather than what the datacenter says left, it is what the output-accounting rule already asks for, and its one new premise (the device's record is in each verification phase's statement) is the two-stage form of a premise the deployed one-stage guarantee already takes; it changes what the two-stage verifier checks, which is why it is Daniel's, it is about 700 to 900 lines of Lean with no listed guarantee's wording changed, and until it is built every two-stage figure in gigabytes rests on (A).

def gated (ok : Bool) (V : Verifier FlockDeploy.Coin) : Verifier FlockDeploy.Coin where
  k := V.k
  next := fun x as cs => bif ok then V.next x as cs else .ret .rej

def parseWired (x : Msg) : Option AuditStatement :=
  (parse h x).map fun s => { s with prog := (bitsProgs h.ms).wired ω keep }

def twoGated (ok : Bool) (s : AuditStatement) : Option Design.Two := bif ok then twoWired h ω s else none

noncomputable def baseWired (ok : Bool) : Code :=
  { h.frame with
    V := gated ok (V h)
    parse := parseWired h ω keep
    scopeCheck := fun x => ((parseWired h ω keep x).bind (partitionWired h ω)).isSome
    partition := partitionWired h ω
    reveal := revealWired h ω keep h.frame
    -- stage2, checked, rounds, session, reveals, sessions, tables, unitN₀, innerN₀: `base h`'s, word for word

noncomputable abbrev codeWired (ok : Bool) : Code :=
  codeTwoStage (baseWired h ω keep ok) (reg h) (fun _ => L) (fun _ => h.stage * L) (fun _ => coinByte)
    (fun _ => h.stage) (stageOrderWired h ω keep ok) fun _ => stageByte

def wiredOk : Bool :=
  (List.range h.ms.length).all (templateOk h) && h.ms.all memberOk && writersFirst h && noReturnedWired h &&
    wiresMove h

noncomputable abbrev codeConnected : Code := codeWired h (wireMap h) (returned h) (wiredOk h)
def twoConnected : AuditStatement → Option Design.Two := twoGated h (wireMap h) (wiredOk h)
noncomputable def rsConnected : (x : Msg) → (Fin ((codeConnected h).V.k x) → FlockDeploy.Coin) → List ℕ :=
  rsWired h (wireMap h) (returned h) (wiredOk h)
```

def traceInputs (s : AuditStatement) (val : ℕ → Option Bool) (g : ℕ) : Option Bool :=
  if s.prog.gates[g]? = some .input then val g else none

def traceServed (s : AuditStatement) (val : ℕ → Option Bool) : Fin s.prog.outs.length → Bool :=
  fun i => (s.prog.read val s.prog.outs[i]).getD false

noncomputable def influenceTwoAt (s : AuditStatement) (Pt : Partition) (d : Design.Two) (δ : ℝ)
    (a : ℕ → Option Bool) : Finset (Fin s.prog.outs.length → Bool) :=
  Finset.univ.filter fun y => ∃ val : ℕ → Option Bool, traceInputs s val = a ∧
    (∃ ι : ℕ → ℕ → Bool, footprintAt s Pt d.part val ι ∈ d.M Pt δ) ∧ traceServed s val = y

def ExfilRegTwoX (H : Msg → Msg) (L : CompiledTwo Coin A) : Prop :=
  L.KSRegTwoX H ∧
    (∀ x, L.Scope x → ∀ (Ω : Type) [Fintype Ω] [Nonempty Ω] (P : Prover Ω),
      ∀ s Pt d, L.parse x = some s → L.partition s = some Pt → L.two s = some d → ∀ δ : ℝ, 0 ≤ δ →
        Pr (fun p : Ω × (Fin (L.V.k x) → Coin) => (run H P L.V x p.1 p.2).out = .acc ∧
            traceServed s (L.regValX H P x) ∉ influenceTwoAt s Pt d δ (traceInputs s (L.regValX H P x))) ≤
          δ + L.εregTwoX H x P) ∧
    ∀ x s Pt d (a : ℕ → Option Bool), L.parse x = some s → L.partition s = some Pt → L.two s = some d →
      InScopeTwo Pt d s → ∀ δ : ℝ,
        (influenceTwoAt s Pt d δ a).card ≤ ∑ T ∈ admissibleTwo Pt d δ, 2 ^ bitsOf s Pt T

**What I take "run" to mean:** one execution of the served workload with its audits, under one registered deployment and one certifier key. "The same digest in two runs" is then two such executions whose case for a subprotocol has one digest, so that the composite's binding cannot tell which run that case came from.

**How the binding is made** (your 22:03Z half, confirmed in Lean). A subprotocol's digest is `P.digest` of its decoded commitment (`CoreProtocol/Protocol.lean` T:58, T:99; M:63, M:104). A composite's commitment is `bind` of (id, digest) in the order of the ids, and it is its own digest (`CoreComposition/Product.lean` T:72, T:143; M:78, M:149); `judge` refuses a commitment that is not that binding (T:92; M:98). `composite.py` computes the same (T:98, T:135; M:92, M:129). The public file's per-case `commitment` is the case's commitment bytes, not the digest (T:177-178; M:171-172).

### The table

| Subprotocol | Its digest is over | Is it the commitment itself? | One digest in two runs? |
|---|---|---|---|
| sampled proofs (`verity/sampled-proofs/one-stage/v1`, `verity/sampled-proofs/v1`) | the run's registration record | no: SHA-512 of it | only if the same record is registered twice |
| the inference-only policy (`verity/inference-only/v0`) | the same record | no: the same SHA-512 | as sampled proofs: it is the same digest |
| PoUW's period (`verity/pouw/period/v1`) | the auditor's whole ledger | no: SHA-512 of its bytes | yes, when both are read from one copy of the ledger |
| the network certifier's period (`verity/certifier/v0`) | the registration records of its compute audits and its execution phases | no: SHA-512 of them | rows form: no. Clock form: only if every record is registered twice |
| PoUS's run (`verity/pous/p2/v4/run`) | the store's setup outputs | no: SHA-512 of them | yes: every run on one store |
| the remote bandwidth audit (`verity/remote-bandwidth/p2/v0`) | the store's registration file and its plan | no: SHA-512 of it | yes: every session on one registered store |
| the wipe (`verity/wipe/v0`) | the server, the session id and the wipe's parameters | no: SHA-512 of them | no: the session id is 32 fresh bytes |
| the composite itself | its subprotocols' digests | yes | exactly when every subprotocol's is |

### What the ties already hold

A tie compares values the named subprotocols read off their own cases with each other, and refuses when they differ (`Tie.lean` `Tie.strays`, T:21-28; M:25). It never compares a case with anything outside the composite, so **no tie holds a case to a run.** What the ties do is carry one subprotocol's value to another:

- the policy and sampled proofs on one record (`same`, every product);
- PoUW's windows on that record (`windows`: remote and remote-network at T; onsite too at M);
- the certifier's compute audits on that record (`egress`: the two remote-network products, T only);
- PoUS and the remote bandwidth audit on one store (`store`, onsite; `CoreOnsite.lean` T:51-56; M:73-80). Both sides of it are one a store, so it adds nothing about the run.

So wherever the registration record is one a run (row 1), an accepted composite's PoUW windows and, in remote-network, its certifier's compute audits are that run's too. Nothing carries it to PoUS, the remote bandwidth audit or the wipe.

- **`served_verdicts.py`.** `sampled_proofs_row` is on T only.

The params are the verifier's own copies and hold the per-run value for PoUS (`session_id`), the wipe (`server`, `session`), the certifier (`session`, `first`, `windows`) and PoUW (`name`). The record would hold the composite's `params_sha512` of each case to the params it knows for its own run, beside the digest.
